transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-12-17
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Khan, Ben Ortiz, Lena Park (Redwood); Maya Patel, Tom Erickson, Priya Rao, Carlos Mendes (DataBridge)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be noisy): We walked through current POC integration using the Redwood SDK, function calls are wired up to a tools layer that hits their appointment DB, structured output needs stronger schema enforcement, discussed returning strict JSON vs free text and error handling; also talked about dedicated vs hosted for perf and compliance.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha Khan: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for taking time. quick agenda - status update, review SDK snippets, go over structured output schema, and then next steps.
[00:08] Maya Patel: hey, thanks. we had ben's example running yesterday, we wired it into our test service that proxies calls to appointments, saw some mismatches in the JSON.
[00:15] Ben Ortiz: yeah i think that's on me — the example used the quick parser which returns a python dict, and in our case the customers service expects a strict schema with fields date, patient_id, action. i'm going to update to show function calling with explicit response schema.
[00:27] Tom Erickson: can you show where the failure came from? we saw a few tokens like "appt" instead of "appointment" and the date format was off.
[00:36] Ben Ortiz: sure, i can paste the snippet after the call but essentially right now the model is returning freeform text for the action field, the plan is to use Redwood's structured output mode and function-calls so the runtime enforces JSON schema.
[00:48] Priya Rao: are you recommending function calls for every interaction? what's the perf impact?
[00:54] Lena Park: not necessarily for every interaction, but for canonical operations where you need a typed response it's helpful. overhead is minimal — we've seen delta of like 10-20ms per request for the function-call plumbing versus freeform text, but that depends on SDK and network. with our batching and KV cache you can offset cost.
[01:11] Maya Patel: and what about retries/partial outputs? we had a case where the model returned truncated JSON, the parser failed and the app crashed.
[01:20] Ben Ortiz: that is an important point. recommended pattern is: enable structured_output enforcement in the call, validate against schema on the client side, then fallback to a re-call with a stricter temperature or a clarification prompt. we can show an example of using tool-calls with a small wrapper that validates and retries.
[01:35] Tom Erickson: this ties to our error-handling model, yes. also curious about quantization differences — does Redwood have guidance on picking model variants for structured outputs?
[01:45] Lena Park: yes, for structured outputs we generally prefer full-precision or Q4_xxx quantizations when you need deterministic JSON fields; heavy quant can occasionally garble tokens in edge-cases. we'll include recommendations in the SDK doc.
[01:58] Carlos Mendes: on the security side, a few questions — how are API keys rotated with dedicated and with private? and how does KMS tie in if we use Redwood Private?
[02:07] Aisha Khan: good questions. for hosted API key rotation you can rotate keys in console and use short-lived tokens; for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support envelope encryption. we'll share the SOC2 + KMS integration doc after this call.
[02:18] Carlos Mendes: and audit logs? we need per-request logs for a 90 day retention window.
[02:23] Ben Ortiz: Redwood Console can export per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns; for Private deployments we can push logs to customer's logging endpoint or S3-compatible store. we'll include sample log export configs.
[02:33] Maya Patel: back to integration — can Redwood SDK call our internal tools? we have an internal service that enriches patient records.
[02:39] Ben Ortiz: yes that maps to the tool-calling pattern; define your tool interface (name, params, return schema) and register it with the SDK. Example: a tool called `enrich_patient` with params {patient_id, fields}. the model will emit a function call which you can execute and then feed back the tool result as context.
[02:54] Priya Rao: any concerns about latency when chaining tools? our enrichment service is synchronous and takes 100-200ms.
[03:02] Lena Park: chaining adds round-trips. common approach is to parallelize non-dependent tools or cache tool outputs; Redwood's built-in KV cache helps when you call the same enrichment repeatedly. if enrichment is critical path consider co-locating or using asynchronous callbacks.
[03:20] Tom Erickson: what about dedicated capacity? if we go with dedicated, can we pin a model and avoid cold-start latencies?
[03:27] Aisha Khan: yes dedicated gives predictable throughput and you can pin model versions. cold starts are much lower. we can also configure burst capacity for peak windows.
[03:34] Maya Patel: perfect. for the SDK example, can you include Node and Python both and show the function signature + structured output schema?
[03:40] Ben Ortiz: absolutely. i'll add both and include a sample JSON Schema and a naive client-side validator snippet.
[03:47] Tom Erickson: also want to measure end-to-end: our expected 95th p99 should be under 350ms for simple queries — is that realistic?
[03:55] Lena Park: depending on model size and region it's doable on dedicated infra. on hosted, p95 of 350ms might be tight for larger models, but our optimized kernels and batching can help. we'll run a benchmark to validate.
[04:07] Priya Rao: about costs — if we enable structured output enforcement and multiple retries, cost could spike. how should we balance?
[04:13] Ben Ortiz: tune temperature, use shorter prompts, enable prefix caching for conversational flows, and set a retry policy with a small max retries. Optimize for sketchy cases first: if a prompt frequently fails JSON, add a lightweight system message guiding the model to always return valid JSON.
[04:29] Maya Patel: are there known gotchas when using structured output with function calls and streaming? we stream responses to the UI for progressive UX.
[04:36] Lena Park: streaming with function calls is supported but you need to handle partial payloads client-side. recommend buffering until a complete JSON object is received or use the end-of-stream marker. we'll include a small client example.
[04:50] Tom Erickson: okay, can you repeat the concrete deliverables?
[04:53] Aisha Khan: sure - Ben will send updated SDK snippets for Node + Python with function-calls and structured output; Lena will add quantization recommendations and streaming patterns; we'll send SOC2/KMS/VPC notes; DataBridge will run the 1k request benchmark and share logs.
[05:06] Maya Patel: sounds good. one small thing: in the last test we saw occasional mis-attribution of speaker names in logs, just noise but we want clean transcripts for our internal review.
[05:14] Ben Ortiz: noted — the transcript engine from Fireflies sometimes mislabels, we'll attach the raw recording as well.
[05:20] Carlos Mendes: one final Q - does Redwood support SAML SSO and RBAC for console access?
[05:25] Aisha Khan: yes SAML SSO is supported and RBAC with role templates. we'll share details in the security doc.
[05:31] Priya Rao: ok thanks everyone.
[05:33] Aisha Khan: thanks all, we'll follow up with the items.
